explanations.explanation: True, friend. Right after the perfume line, the Teacher says “one’s day of death is better than his day of birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1). That one is heavy, and I think it's meant to make a person slow down and think. He's just getting started on his list.

It's a surprising line, so I get why you'd doubt it. But the Teacher really does say it: “one’s day of death is better than his day of birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1). It comes right after the line about a good name and fine perfume. I think it's a heavy one to sit with, and he doesn't hurry past it.

That's the reason he gives. He says it's better to enter a house of mourning “since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:2). The verse puts it on the living to take it to heart. That's a quiet kind of teaching, and I think it's one worth sitting with.

Money never comes up in that verse, friend. The Teacher just says a house of mourning is better to enter than a house of feasting, and then gives his reason: “since death is the end of every man” (Ecclesiastes 7:2). He adds that “the living should take this to heart.” So the reason is death, and the verse doesn't mention spending.

That's a kind thought, and I think comforting people matters. But it isn't the reason this verse gives. The Teacher says a house of mourning is better to enter “since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:2). His reason is that death comes to everyone.

It's the other way around, friend. The Teacher says “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure” (Ecclesiastes 7:4). The wise go with mourning and the fools go with pleasure. It's easy to flip them, since pleasure sounds like the wiser pick at first.

False is right. The verse says “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure” (Ecclesiastes 7:4). So the wise heart sits in the house of mourning, not the house of pleasure. The Teacher is still building on what he said just before about sorrow and the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:3).

Heed is the word. The Teacher says “It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7:5). To heed is to listen and take it in, which is harder than it sounds. A rebuke never comes with a catchy chorus, but he says it's the better thing to listen to.

Ignoring a rebuke is a very human move, like hitting snooze on an alarm that's trying to help you. But the verse says the opposite: “It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7:5). He wants the rebuke heeded and the song of fools set aside.

Repeating a rebuke back like a parrot isn't what he asks for, friend. The verse says “It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7:5). To heed it is to listen and take it in. That's the part that counts.

That's the comparison. The Teacher says “like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:6). Then comes the short line “This too is futile.” It's a picture you can hear, and he uses it for that laughter.

The rebuke of the wise is on the other side of that list, friend. In the verse before, he says it's better to heed a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools (Ecclesiastes 7:5). The crackling thorns are about something else: “so is the laughter of the fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:6). The rebuke is the one he tells us to heed.

Sorrow gets different treatment in this stretch. The Teacher says “Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:3). The crackling thorns aren't about sorrow. They go with “the laughter of the fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:6).

True. The whole verse reads “Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:7). The two warnings sit together in one line. Both are about what can wreck a person on the inside.

The bribe is right there in the same verse, friend. The Teacher says “Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:7). Extortion goes with the wise man and the bribe goes with the heart. It's a short verse, so it's easy to blink and miss half of it.

Patient wins. The Teacher says “The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one” (Ecclesiastes 7:8). He puts patient and proud side by side and picks patient. Waiting well is hard, and I'm still working on it myself.

Proud is the one he sets lower, friend. The verse says “a patient spirit is better than a proud one” (Ecclesiastes 7:8). So the proud spirit is on the losing end of that comparison. Patient is the one he calls better.

Bold sounds good, like an extra scoop of chocolate chips, but it isn't in this verse. The Teacher only sets two spirits side by side: “a patient spirit is better than a proud one” (Ecclesiastes 7:8). Patient is the one he calls better. Bold never gets a turn.

Fool is the word. The verse says “Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:9). Picture anger getting comfy in a lap like it pays rent there. The Teacher says that lap belongs to a fool.

A king would make it sound fancier, but that's not the word. The verse says “Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:9). Anger settles in the lap of a fool, and the Teacher doesn't mention kings here.

A stranger isn't in this verse, friend. The Teacher says “Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:9). The word is fool. He's talking about what happens in our own spirit, not about someone we don't know.

It's the opposite, friend. The Teacher says “Do not say, ‘Why were the old days better than these?’ For it is unwise of you to ask about this” (Ecclesiastes 7:10). He calls the question unwise. Even I spent years in a junk drawer, and I wouldn't trade today for it.

False is right. The Teacher says “Do not say, ‘Why were the old days better than these?’ For it is unwise of you to ask about this” (Ecclesiastes 7:10). So he doesn't call the question wise. He calls it unwise. I'll admit it's a tempting question to ask.

Life is the word. The Teacher says “wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner” (Ecclesiastes 7:12). Money is the comparison, but the verse says wisdom is what preserves life. That's a big advantage for something you can't count in a cookie jar.

Wealth is close, because the verse does bring up money. But it says wisdom is a shelter “like money,” and then “wisdom preserves the life of its owner” (Ecclesiastes 7:12). The money is the comparison. What wisdom preserves is the owner's life.

A good name was the Teacher's opening line in this passage (Ecclesiastes 7:1), so I see why it stuck with you. But this verse ends differently: “wisdom preserves the life of its owner” (Ecclesiastes 7:12). The word is life, not name.

Straighten is the word. The Teacher says “Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?” (Ecclesiastes 7:13). It's a question, and he leaves it hanging. I think the quiet after it is part of the point.

Break is a strong word, but it's not in this verse. The Teacher asks “Who can straighten what He has bent?” (Ecclesiastes 7:13). The question is about straightening what God has bent. Nothing in it is about breaking.
Hiding isn't what the Teacher asks about, friend. The verse says “Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?” (Ecclesiastes 7:13). Straighten is the word that goes with bent.
Be joyful, plain and simple. The Teacher says “In the day of prosperity, be joyful” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). No extra assignment comes with it. When a good day shows up, he says to be glad in it.
Storing up is a sensible idea, but it's not what this verse says. The Teacher says “In the day of prosperity, be joyful” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). Joy is the instruction he gives for the good day.

Staying on guard isn't in this verse, friend. The Teacher says “In the day of prosperity, be joyful” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). That's the whole instruction for the good day. He saves the word “consider” for the day of adversity.

True. The verse says “God has made one of these along with the other” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). The one he means is the day of adversity, made along with the day of prosperity. That's what the Teacher says to consider when the hard day comes.

The verse says it outright, friend. In the day of adversity, the Teacher says to consider this: “God has made one of these along with the other” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). The two days are the day of prosperity and the day of adversity. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: So a man cannot discover what comes after him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. The Teacher says “God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). He doesn't say more than that. We don't get to see what's coming, and I think that's worth a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: So people learn to save up for hard times
explanations.explanation: Saving up is sensible, but the verse doesn't give that as the reason. It says “God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). The reason is that a man cannot discover what will come after him.

explanations.answer: So the proud are humbled and brought down low
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason this verse gives, friend. The Teacher says “God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him” (Ecclesiastes 7:14). Pride isn't mentioned in it. The reason is that a man cannot discover what comes after him.
